title: Choosing wood for whittling
subtitle: A guide to species, state, and grain for knife work
excerpt: The species and state of the wood is the single biggest variable in how a whittling project turns out. This article covers the beginner shortlist, what to look for in a board or branch, and which species to avoid until the knife skills are established.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
The direction in which the wood fibres run, from root to tip in a tree. Cuts made with the grain are clean; cuts made against the grain tend to tear.

content.text: Most beginners pick up a piece of wood and start cutting without considering the species or state. This article covers what to look for when choosing whittling wood, why it matters, and which species are worth starting with.
What makes a wood good for whittling

Four properties matter for knife work. First, hardness: the wood should be soft enough that a sharp knife enters without requiring heavy force, but hard enough that it holds detail without crumbling. Second, grain evenness: straight, even
grain
makes the cut direction predictable. Third, texture: fine-grained woods produce a cleaner knife finish than coarse-grained. Fourth, stability:
seasoned wood
at stable moisture content does not crack or warp as the piece is worked.
The beginner shortlist

Lime (Tilia europaea): the traditional carver's wood. Very fine grain, soft, cuts in any direction without significant tearing. The best choice for figures and relief carving where detail is more important than strength. Lime boards are available from specialist suppliers; lime is not a standard builders'-merchant timber.

Pine: widely available from any builders' merchant in PAR board. Soft, fast-cutting, and very forgiving of imprecise angles. The resin content means it is not food-safe for prolonged wet contact, but it is excellent for practice pieces, decorative items, and anything that won't touch food. Knot-free sections only.

Sycamore: a very good general-purpose whittling wood. Fine grain, white, food-safe, and available from timber merchants as PAR board. Slightly harder than lime but still very comfortable under a sharp knife. The grain on some sycamore boards is interlocked (wavy), which requires more attention to direction.

Ash: strong in thin section, food-safe, open-grained. A good step up from pine for functional pieces. The open grain is visible in the finished surface; some people like this quality, others prefer the finer texture of sycamore or lime.
Woods to avoid at the start
Oak: hard, with medullary rays that splinter across the grain when a cut goes wrong. Not a beginner species.
Beech: fine grain, but significantly harder than sycamore or ash. Requires frequent sharpening and more force per cut; less forgiving of dull edges.

Exotic hardwoods in general: harder, denser, and often more expensive to waste on practice. Some (teak, iroko, certain rosewoods) produce irritant dust and should not be cut with a hand knife without respiratory protection.

Unseasoned timber from a builders' merchant: green softwood from a builders' merchant is often 20 per cent or more moisture content and will warp and crack as it dries. Buy kiln-dried PAR board from a reputable merchant, not construction-grade timber.
Sourcing without a timber merchant

Pine PAR board from a hardware store is the easiest starting point. Look for sections without knots. For sycamore, lime, or ash, a specialist timber merchant is the most reliable source; many sell short lengths specifically for craft use. Tree surgeons sometimes give away sections of interesting species: ask for hardwood from healthy trees, not from diseased or chemically-treated trees. Dry and store any green material for at least a year before whittling.
Checking a board before buying
Sight along the board. A twist or bow in the board does not improve with whittling.
Check the ends for checking (radial cracks). End checks in a board are normal but their depth tells you whether the board has been seasoned properly or dried too fast.
Count the knots in the section you intend to use. A knot in the blade section of a letter opener or pendant is likely to cause the piece to fail.
